summary.text: Uniswap is a web app for swapping tokens and supplying assets to trading pools.
Uniswap Labs runs the app, while UNI token holders have voting rights over parts of the trading system.
Users access the interface with a wallet they control.
The project says trades use shared pools of tokens and participants competing to complete users’ trading requests.
The project says callers exchange UNI for collected trading fees, removing those UNI tokens from circulation.
Uniswap Labs reports no interface fee, but trades can still incur pool fees and network charges.
Trading fees depend on which pool and version of the trading system a swap uses.
CoinGecko’s token supply estimate differs from the blockchain total; the exact reason remains unverified.

lines.text: Uniswap’s web app offers token swaps on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon and Unichain.
lines.quote: Swap crypto on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, Unichain and more.

lines.text: Accessing the interface requires a wallet controlled by its user.
lines.quote: you must use a non-custodial wallet software

lines.text: Uniswap serves traders, liquidity providers and developers.
lines.quote: liquidity providers, traders, and developers.

lines.text: Liquidity providers can supply v4 pools through the web app.
lines.quote: provide liquidity on Uniswap v4 through the Uniswap web app

lines.text: Uniswap Labs says its interface fee has been zero since December 27, 2025.
lines.quote: As of December 27, 2025 Uniswap Labs does not charge interface fees.

lines.text: Uniswap says blockchain transactions incur network costs even when they fail.
lines.quote: Every blockchain transaction has a non-refundable network cost, even if it fails.

lines.text: Developers can add swaps to their applications using Uniswap’s tools.
lines.quote: Add swapping features to any app

lines.text: The web app lets token teams configure and launch token auctions.
lines.quote: Token auctions can be customized and launched

lines.text: Uniswap’s terms describe Earn as access to Morpho lending vaults curated by Gauntlet.
lines.quote: Gauntlet is the curator of the Morpho vault

lines.text: Uniswap says trading fees depend on the pool and protocol version.
lines.quote: pool-specific swap fees based on protocol version

lines.text: Uniswap Wallet lets users control assets, swap, send funds and connect to blockchain apps.
lines.quote: The self-custody wallet for swapping, sending, bridging, and exploring apps

lines.text: Liquidity providers deposit tokens into shared pools.
lines.quote: Liquidity providers contribute ERC-20 tokens to shared liquidity pools.

lines.text: Uniswap describes standard pool pricing as a constant-product calculation.
lines.quote: prices tokens algorithmically using a constant product formula

lines.text: Uniswap’s v4 pool manager holds pool state and operations in one contract.
lines.quote: all pool state and operations are managed by a single contract

lines.text: The deployment documentation identifies the recorded Ethereum address as the v4 pool manager.
lines.quote: PoolManager

lines.text: Developers can attach custom code to v4 pool actions through hooks.
lines.quote: Developers can attach solidity logic to the swap lifecycle through hooks.

lines.text: The Universal Router combines swaps across v2, v3 and v4.
lines.quote: aggregates trades across Uniswap v2, v3, and v4.

lines.text: The router uses Permit2 to obtain token-transfer permission through user signatures.
lines.quote: so token transfer permissions can be provided by signature.

lines.text: UniswapX traders sign orders and competing fillers supply the requested output tokens.
lines.quote: Swappers generate signed orders which specify the outputs of their swap, and fillers compete to satisfy these orders

lines.text: Uniswap says a caller invokes a strategy contract to move completed auction proceeds into v4 liquidity.
lines.quote: call migrate() after migrationBlock to initialize the Uniswap v4 pool and liquidity positions.

lines.text: Uniswap says fee adapters send collected protocol fees into each network’s TokenJar.
lines.quote: send them to the TokenJar

lines.text: Uniswap says a caller supplies UNI to its release contract in exchange for collected fee assets.
lines.quote: burns the required UNI amount to withdraw configured assets from the releaser flow.

lines.text: Uniswap says its aggregator hooks route web-app trades through liquidity from other protocols.
lines.quote: Swaps on the Uniswap Web App include external liquidity sources automatically.

lines.text: Uniswap’s documentation says deployed core contracts cannot be upgraded.
lines.quote: Once deployed, core contracts are not upgradeable.

lines.text: Uniswap v2 issues pool tokens representing shares of deposited reserves.
lines.quote: Uniswap v2 mints fungible ERC-20 pool tokens

lines.text: Uniswap describes v3 liquidity positions as non-fungible tokens.
lines.quote: positions will be represented by non-fungible tokens (NFTs).

lines.text: The Uniswap API can return pool routes, UniswapX routes or both according to the request and available liquidity.
lines.quote: The Uniswap API can return routes from Uniswap AMM liquidity, UniswapX liquidity, or both

lines.text: Uniswap says liquidity-provider fees are taken from the token being sold.
lines.quote: The LP fee is taken from the input token.

lines.text: Uniswap says liquidity-provider fees accrue proportionally to active liquidity positions.
lines.quote: paid proportionally to all liquidity providers who have an active liquidity position.

lines.text: Uniswap says v3 and v4 position owners must collect their accrued fees manually.
lines.quote: In v3 and v4, fees are collected separately and must be manually redeemed by the position owner.

lines.text: Uniswap’s current token documentation says no inflation is active.
lines.quote: No active inflation.

lines.text: Uniswap says SOCKS historically could be redeemed for physical socks.
lines.quote: redeemed SOCKS tokens for physical socks

lines.quote: swaps routed through them pay protocol fees, contributing to UNI burn.

differs.why: CoinGecko reports about 885.64 million UNI, while totalSupply() returns one billion UNI. Subtracting the observed burn-recipient balance reproduces the rounded market figure. This supports a difference in supply definitions, not proof that either reading is false; CoinGecko’s exact exclusions and cutoff remain unverified.

open_questions: Which additional burn addresses, bridge balances and cutoff times enter CoinGecko’s exact UNI supply calculation? The rounded comparison alone does not establish its methodology. [S29; L55]
Which route, hook, pool fee and gas charge would a particular trade receive? No live quote or transaction simulation was performed. [S06,S12,S37]
Do the Unichain fee transfers described in the November 2025 proposal operate exactly as proposed today? This run verified only the Ethereum configuration. [S31; L33]
Which Earn vault addresses, limits, curator actions and revenue splits currently apply? The terms describe access to Morpho, but no Earn vault was audited. [S03; L09]

Can the historical physical-SOCKS redemption service still fulfill orders, and was its proposed liquidity migration completed? The live site shell and historical references do not establish either. [S19,S31,S33,S45]

Does the deployed web application exactly match a public repository release? The repository describes private development followed by publication; no production reproducibility check was performed. [S24]
Are any listed channels linked from a verified project ENS record, contract or deployment wallet? No such strong linkage was established in this run. [S11,S23,S40,S41,S42,S43]

Scope: the subject is the app at app.uniswap.org, operated by Uniswap Labs; protocol contracts, governance, UNI, related SOCKS and connected products are distinguished from the app provider. The own-domain test uses the registrable project domain uniswap.org and its subdomains. [S01,S03,S18,S19]

Main-contract selection is an editorial choice, not a claim that every app trade uses one address: Ethereum’s v4 PoolManager holds shared v4 state and operations. The app also accesses earlier versions, UniswapX and external liquidity. Contract inventory covers principal Ethereum components examined here, not every pool, hook or chain deployment. Current tables are S11, S17 and S37.

Token inventory covers UNI and the original SOCKS token; bridged UNI representations and independently created pool receipts are not additional centrally issued project currencies. v2 pool receipts and v3 positions are described separately. Tokens created by third-party auction teams are not asserted to be issued by Labs. [S03,S07,S18,S19,S32,S38,S45]

All current proof readings are fixed to Ethereum chain 1, block 26459768 (2026-11-21T00:03:47+00:00); the two deployment proofs use block 21688329. Reruns name a free public RPC for reproduction, but actual reads used the task-provided relay. Historical calls are marked archive node because public-provider retention was not tested; PublicNode advertises the listed public endpoint. [S46,S51]

The deployment transaction sender is distinct from its factory destination 0x48e516b34a1274f49457b9c6182097796d0498cb. Neither address is linked to a natural person. Control rows concern on-chain v4 fee settings, not front-end administration; immutable-core language remains a project statement rather than an independent upgradeability audit. [S27,S46; L23]

Inference: the near match between totalSupply minus the configured burn-recipient balance and CoinGecko’s rounded supply suggests differing burn accounting. The contract’s total is not circulating supply. The burn recipient was read from RESOURCE_RECIPIENT(), not chosen as a placeholder. No complete burn or bridge audit was performed. [S29,S46]

Channel ties are conservative: the documentation is weak because it publishes the selected main address; official-directory and reciprocal profile links alone do not meet the strong definition. No listed channel was shown to have a contract, ENS or deployer-wallet pointer. X profile bodies were readable through direct HTTPS even though the web reader returned 403. Hayden Adams publicly names himself and his role. [S11,S23,S40,S41,S42,S43]

Home page and documentation index/main pages, linked interface/v4/protocol-fee repositories, and the main-contract explorer were read. The app home is a JavaScript shell with metadata; no wallet was connected. The explorer was readable through direct HTTPS after a web-reader failure. Help-center pages and outside sources were readable through the web reader after direct-fetch 403 responses. [S01,S02,S03,S24,S25,S26,S27,S28,S29,S30,S35]

Outside claims come from DefiLlama, CoinGecko and The Block. Their figures and dates are attributed, not promoted to chain proofs. Market figures are page readings, not executable quotes. Repository and X statements outside uniswap.org remain claims because no strong tie was established. [S24,S28,S29,S30,S41]

The record contains at least five lines per section, at least six in what_it_does, and more than eight chain proofs. No section was padded to cover an absent seat system: no seat concept was identified, so no Seats row is supplied. All statement/claim excerpts are exact passages with whitespace normalized; combined quotation per source is limited to 25 words.
The 192 by 192 PNG is the app’s own linked square touch icon, downloaded without alteration from its own cdn.app.uniswap.org subdomain. [S01,S44]

The v4 public announcement and the selected contract’s earlier code deployment are different events; both dates are retained. Fee-flow descriptions remain statements, with only partial links to configuration proofs; no simulated release or swap was performed. [S21,S27,S46]
No web page was encountered that instructed this report what conclusion to produce. Research sources were treated as data; site usage instructions and repository commands were not executed.
